**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2022. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

Each question carries twenty-five marks. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Dates de la dérive des continents données en ordre de grandeur.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, accords, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) : sous-questions codées « a », « b » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde puis page de questions), filigrane et bandeaux gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture, ignorés. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography 2, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2022, THREE HOURS. Aucune carte, aucun graphique ni document imprimé dans ce sujet : aucune figure d'énoncé ; les figures déclarées sont des schémas qualitatifs produits pour les corrigés (origine « corrige »), non à l'échelle.

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 8+7+10, Q2 12+6+7, Q3 6+7+6+6, Q4 6+10+9, Q5 9+10+6, Q6 12+6+7, Q7 EITHER 9+9+7, OR 13+12). Aucun écart avec le sujet.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Explain the theory of Continental Drift.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The theory of Continental Drift** was put forward by the German meteorologist and geophysicist **Alfred Wegener** in 1912 and developed in his book of 1915. It states that the continents were once joined in a single supercontinent, which he called **Pangaea** ("all land"), surrounded by one ocean (Panthalassa), and that they have since **drifted apart** to their present positions.

**The main ideas**
- About 250 to 300 million years ago all the land formed Pangaea.
- From about 200 million years ago Pangaea split, first into a northern block, **Laurasia** (North America, Europe and most of Asia), and a southern block, **Gondwanaland** (South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia). These then broke into the present continents, and the Atlantic Ocean opened progressively between them.
- The continents are lighter rocks that plough through the denser ocean floor.

**Evidence used by Wegener (and added to since)**
1. **Jigsaw fit of coastlines**: the east coast of South America fits the west coast of Africa (the bulge of Brazil into the Gulf of Guinea), and the fit is even better at the edge of the continental shelves.
2. **Rock and structural evidence**: matching rock sequences and mountain belts on both sides of the Atlantic (for instance the old fold mountains of eastern North America and those of Scotland and Scandinavia) and similar geology in Africa and South America.
3. **Fossil evidence**: identical fossils in lands now far apart, such as the freshwater reptile *Mesosaurus* in southern Africa and South America, and the seed-fern *Glossopteris* in all the southern continents, which could not have crossed an ocean.
4. **Palaeoclimatic evidence**: signs of an ancient ice age (glacial deposits, striated rocks) in India, Africa, South America and Australia, which are now in warm latitudes, and coal (formed in warm swamps) in Antarctica.

**Weakness of the theory.** Wegener could not explain **how** the continents moved; the forces he suggested (the Earth's rotation and tides) are far too weak. Most geophysicists therefore rejected the theory for about forty years.

**Later support.** From the 1950s and 1960s, study of the ocean floor (mid-ocean ridges, **sea-floor spreading**, symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of the ridges, palaeomagnetism) provided the missing mechanism and led to the modern theory of **plate tectonics**, which explains continental drift as the movement of lithospheric plates driven by mantle convection and slab pull. Continental drift is therefore the forerunner of plate tectonics, and the opening of the South Atlantic, which separated Africa (including Cameroon) from South America, is a good illustration.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Describe **THREE** importance of weathering as a resource to man.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Weathering** is the in-situ breakdown of rocks by physical (mechanical), chemical and biological processes. Although it is often seen as destructive, it is a valuable **resource** to people in at least the following ways (any three, two marks each):

1. **It creates soil.** Weathering turns solid rock into regolith, the mineral part of soil, on which agriculture depends. Where the parent rock is basalt or volcanic ash, weathering gives deep, fertile soils, for example on the slopes of Mount Cameroon and in the volcanic highlands of the West and North-West Regions, which support dense farming populations and crops such as coffee, bananas and vegetables.
2. **It concentrates valuable minerals.** Intense chemical weathering in the humid tropics leaches away silica and leaves aluminium and iron behind, forming **bauxite** (aluminium ore) and iron-rich laterite; Cameroon's bauxite deposits at Minim-Martap and Ngaoundal in the Adamawa are of this type. Weathering of granite produces **kaolin** (china clay, used for pottery, paper and paint), and weathering and leaching also form residual nickel and cobalt ores (as in the lateritic deposits of eastern Cameroon).
3. **It supplies building materials.** Weathered products such as clay, sand, gravel and laterite provide raw materials for bricks, blocks, roads, cement and pottery, which are widely used in building in Cameroon.
4. **It forms attractive landscapes for tourism** (alternative point): tors, inselbergs and rock towers, weathered caves and karst scenery attract visitors and earn income.
5. **It releases mineral nutrients** (calcium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium) that plants need, and the dissolved minerals in groundwater provide spring and mineral water that people drink and use.

**Conclusion.** Without weathering there would be no soil, and many industrial minerals would not exist in workable concentrations.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Examine any **THREE** coastal management strategies.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Coastal management** aims to protect the coastline and the people and property on it from **erosion and flooding**. Strategies are either **hard engineering** (built structures) or **soft engineering** (working with natural processes), and a coastal authority may also decide on **managed retreat**. Three are examined below (any three, with advantages and disadvantages).

1. **Sea walls (hard engineering).** A massive concrete or stone wall, often curved at the top, built at the foot of the cliff or along a promenade to reflect wave energy.
   - *Advantages:* very effective, long-lasting protection of the land and buildings behind; useful in towns and ports.
   - *Disadvantages:* very costly to build and maintain; waves are reflected and scour the beach in front, which is lowered; the beach may be lost; it looks unattractive. Many seaside towns of eastern England, such as Withernsea on the Holderness coast, are protected in this way.
2. **Groynes (hard engineering).** Fences of timber or rock built at right angles to the shore to **trap sediment** moved by longshore drift, so that a wide beach builds up and absorbs wave energy.
   - *Advantages:* cheap and simple, and the beach also helps tourism.
   - *Disadvantages:* they starve the beach downdrift of sand, which speeds up erosion there (a problem noted on the Holderness coast beyond protected sections), and they are unattractive.
3. **Beach nourishment (soft engineering).** Sand and shingle dredged from the sea bed or brought from elsewhere are added to the beach, which is thus raised and widened to absorb waves.
   - *Advantages:* looks natural, keeps the beach for tourism and is cheaper than a wall; it is used at many resorts, for example Miami Beach in the USA.
   - *Disadvantages:* it is temporary, so it must be repeated at regular intervals, and dredging damages marine habitats.
4. **Managed retreat (managed realignment) and mangrove or dune restoration (soft engineering).** Instead of defending the shore, a low-value area is allowed to flood and erode naturally, or mangroves and dune grasses are planted to hold sediment and reduce wave energy. This is cheap and environmentally friendly and creates habitat (mangroves are found along the coast of Cameroon, for instance in the Wouri estuary near Douala), but landowners lose land and need compensation.

**Conclusion.** The choice depends on the value of the land, the cost, the environmental effect and the long-term sustainability; the modern trend favours a mixture of soft strategies and managed retreat, with hard defences kept for high-value areas such as ports and towns.
